title: Heap index math + sift skeleton
description: The whiteboard boilerplate for a 0-indexed array heap: parent/child index math plus sift-up and sift-down loops.

conversation.intro: How you'd walk through heap mechanics in an interview when the heap shows up as a subroutine (top-K, median stream, Dijkstra). Each section: what you'd say, then why that move matters. Tap to expand.

sections.title: 1. Why drill this?
sections.prompt: When does heap math actually show up?
sections.say: "A heap is the data structure I reach for whenever I need 'the smallest (or largest) so far' on a stream — top-K, median, Dijkstra's frontier, scheduling. JS has no built-in heap, so in a real interview I'd either write the index math from memory or ask 'can I assume a min-heap helper?'. I want both options ready, so this lesson is the index math (parent / left / right) plus the two sift loops (up for insert, down for pop-root) — the skeleton I'd reproduce on a whiteboard."
sections.why: Most candidates blank on heap mechanics the moment a problem needs more than `arr.sort()`. Treating the three index formulas + two sift loops as ONE memorized unit — not five things — turns 'I forget the parent formula' into 'I have a 25-line block I write down'. That confidence frees attention for the actual problem (which heap, what comparator, when to extract).

sections.title: 2. The common mistakes first
sections.prompt: What goes wrong before you get the canonical right?
sections.say:
"Three failures I'd flag before I start writing:"

• "Mixing up 1-indexed and 0-indexed math. The classic textbook formulas are `parent = i/2`, `left = 2i`, `right = 2i+1` — but those are for **1-indexed** heaps. JS arrays are 0-indexed, so I use `parent = (i-1) >> 1`, `left = 2i+1`, `right = 2i+2`. Different by exactly one."

• "On sift-DOWN, swapping with the WRONG child. If I swap with the larger child of a min-heap, the smaller one stays trapped below — heap property broken. Always swap with the smaller (for min-heap) or larger (for max-heap) child."

• "Forgetting the bounds check on sift-down. The current node might have only a left child, or no children at all. `l < heap.length && heap[l] < heap[s]` covers both: the AND short-circuits if the child slot doesn't exist."
sections.why: Surfacing these failures unprompted signals you've HIT them — interviewers can tell the difference between memorized code and lived code. The 1- vs 0-indexed point is the one most candidates miss because they learned heaps from a textbook diagram that used 1-indexed nodes; saying 'in JS I use the 0-indexed form' shows you've translated the abstraction to your tools.

sections.title: 3. Spot the math
sections.prompt: Why does index arithmetic encode a tree?
sections.say:
"A complete binary tree laid out level-by-level into a flat array makes the parent/child relationship pure arithmetic. Level 0 is index 0 (one node). Level 1 is indices 1, 2 (two nodes). Level 2 is indices 3-6 (four nodes). At every level, a node at index `i` has children at `2i+1` and `2i+2`, and its parent is at `(i-1) >> 1`. No pointers, no allocation per node — the tree shape is implied."

"For the sift loops: sift-UP fires after a push. The new item sits at the tail, possibly smaller than its parent, so I bubble it upward swapping with its parent until either the parent is smaller (heap property restored) or I hit the root (`i === 0`). Sift-DOWN fires after a pop-root: I swap root with the tail, shrink the array, then bubble the now-root downward, always picking the smaller child to swap with — until both children are larger or I run out of children."
sections.why: Naming the structural property — 'complete binary tree → contiguous array' — is what shows you understand WHY the formulas work, not just THAT they do. If the interviewer asks 'what if the tree isn't complete?', you can answer: 'then this representation breaks; you'd need pointers or sparse indices.' Heaps are complete BY CONSTRUCTION (we always fill left-to-right), which is what makes the index math correctness-preserving.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a sift-up and a sift-down on concrete numbers.
sections.intro: "Let me run a push-then-sift-up and a pop-root-then-sift-down through the formulas."

examples.note: Sift-up: 2 lands at index 6, parent at index 2 is 3, 3 > 2 so swap; new index 2, parent at index 0 is 1, 1 < 2 so stop.
Pop-root: swap 1↔7, shrink to [7,5,3,10,8], then sift-down 7 from index 0 — swap with smaller child 3.
examples.trace:
swap heap[0]↔heap[5]=7  pop → heap=[7,5,3,10,8]
j=0  l=1, r=2  smaller child = heap[2]=3 < heap[0]=7 → swap → [3,5,7,10,8]  j=2
j=2  l=5, r=6  both out of bounds → STOP  ✓

examples.note: L3 case — pure parent lookup, no sift needed.

sections.why: The sift-down example is the one to narrate aloud — picking the SMALLER child between 3 (index 2) and 5 (index 1) is the load-bearing move. Choose 5 instead and 3 stays trapped below a 7, violating the invariant. Tracing it on numbers surfaces that decision in a way the code alone doesn't.

sections.title: 5. Edges + pitfalls
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless sift implementation?
sections.say:
"Edges I'd think through:"

• "Heap of size 0 or 1 — push into empty heap: tail is at index 0, the `i > 0` guard stops sift-up immediately. Pop-root on size 1: swap with self, pop, sift-down on empty — bounds check `l < heap.length` blocks both child checks."

• "Equal values — comparison is `>` not `>=`, so equal-value parent/child means no swap. That's correct: equal values trivially satisfy the heap property and unnecessary swaps cost time."

• "Sift-down with only a LEFT child — common when the heap has an odd number of nodes. The `r < heap.length` check on the right guards it; we'd compare against left only."

• "Duplicates — heaps handle duplicates fine; the only catch is that a custom comparator must be a total order (no `a == b` returning ambiguous), otherwise sift loops may bounce."

• "Forgetting to `break` when `s === j` on sift-down — without it the loop is infinite. The `break` is what says 'this node is already smaller than both children — stop'."
sections.why: The size-1 pop-root edge is the one that bites under timing pressure: you swap root with tail, then your shrink is `heap.pop()`, leaving an empty array — and sift-down on index 0 of an empty array would NaN-compare against `heap[l]` (undefined). The two `l < heap.length` / `r < heap.length` guards are not paranoia, they're the empty-heap correctness proof. Calling that out shows you've thought past the happy path.

sections.title: 6. Complexity
sections.prompt: What's the cost of these operations and how would you defend it?
sections.say:
"Per operation:"

• "Sift-up: at most one swap per tree level, and a complete binary tree of n nodes has ⌊log₂(n)⌋ + 1 levels. So sift-up is O(log n) — the level count grows logarithmically with size."

• "Sift-down: same argument from the root downward — at most one swap per level, so O(log n) as well."

• "Push and pop-root are O(log n) each. `peek` (read heap[0]) is O(1)."

• "Building a heap from n elements via repeated push is O(n log n), but bottom-up `heapify` — sift-down from index `(n/2)-1` down to 0 — is O(n). The trick is that half the nodes are leaves with 0 work, a quarter sift at most 1 level, an eighth at most 2 levels, and the weighted sum converges to O(n). Worth flagging if the problem builds a heap from a known list."

"If you want me to extend: kth-largest uses this directly — keep a min-heap of size k, push every element, pop when size exceeds k. Final root is the kth largest. O(n log k) total."
sections.why: The bottom-up heapify O(n) result is the one that earns the senior-tier nod — most candidates know push/pop are log n but recite 'building a heap is n log n' by reflex. Knowing the weighted-sum argument shows you've actually done the analysis. Naming kth-largest as the unprompted extension is the standard 'where does this template fire?' move.

notes: A heap is just an array — no node objects. The tree shape is encoded by the index math.
Parent = (i-1) >> 1, left = 2*i+1, right = 2*i+2 — memorize these three formulas.
Sift UP after a push (new item is at the tail). Sift DOWN after a pop-root (move last to index 0, then bubble down).
On sift-down ALWAYS swap with the smaller child — swapping with the larger would leave the smaller child violating the heap property.
MAX-heap variant: same code, flip every comparison (`>` ↔ `<`) in the sift loops. The index math is identical.

alternates.label: Bottom-up heapify (Floyd, O(n))
alternates.when: Reach for this when you're handed an UNORDERED array up front and need to heap-ify it once before draining. Naive 'push every element' is O(n log n); Floyd's bottom-up heapify is O(n) — half the nodes are leaves with zero work, a quarter sift at most one level, and the weighted sum converges to linear. Standard interview answer when the problem starts 'given an unsorted array, find the k smallest…'.
notes: Iterate from `(n>>1) - 1` down to 0 — that's the last node with at least one child. Anything past it is a leaf and already a valid heap of size 1.
The O(n) bound comes from the weighted sum: ~n/2 leaves do 0 work, ~n/4 nodes sift ≤1 level, ~n/8 sift ≤2, etc. The series Σ k·n/2^(k+1) converges to n, not n log n.
On already-min-heap input (like [1,5,3,10,8,7]) every siftDown is a no-op — heapify is idempotent, the output equals the input.

questions.q: For a 0-indexed array heap, the parent of index 7 is:
The left child of index 3 sits at which index?
Why is a heap implemented over an array instead of with node objects?
options: Arrays give O(1) random access to any tree level, which a linked tree can't
Index math (parent/left/right) encodes the tree shape compactly with no pointers
A complete binary tree's traversal order is the same as array iteration, so iteration is free
Arrays guarantee cache locality of sibling nodes, which is what makes sift-down O(log n)
questions.explain: The complete binary tree shape maps perfectly onto contiguous array indices — no parent/child pointers needed.

questions.q: When do you sift UP vs sift DOWN?
options: Sift up on insert (bubble from the tail); sift down on pop-root (bubble from index 0)
Sift down on insert; sift up on pop-root
Sift up for both
Sift down for both
questions.explain: Insert appends at the tail then sifts up. Pop-root swaps root with the tail, shrinks, then sifts down from index 0.

questions.q: On a MIN-heap sift-DOWN, you swap the node with the LARGER of its two children. What breaks?
options: Nothing — the heap re-balances on the next pop because sift-down is idempotent
The smaller child stays below a larger value, violating the heap property at that subtree
Only the root invariant breaks; the rest of the tree stays valid because each subtree is independent
The traversal cost flips from O(log n) to O(n) but the values stay heap-ordered
questions.explain: Promoting the larger child leaves the smaller child sitting under a bigger parent — the min-heap invariant (parent ≤ both children) is violated. Always swap with the SMALLER child.

questions.q: Building a heap by `heapify` (sift-down from the bottom up) over n elements is:
options: O(n log n) — n inserts each O(log n)
O(n) — most nodes are near the leaves and sift down only a few levels
O(n²)
O(log n)
questions.explain: Bottom-up heapify is O(n): half the nodes are leaves (0 work), a quarter sift at most 1 level, etc. — the weighted sum converges to O(n), unlike n separate O(log n) inserts.

questions.q: To turn the min-heap code into a MAX-heap, what's the minimal change?
options: Swap the parent/child index formulas — the tree shape inverts for max-heaps
Flip the comparisons (use `>` where it used `<`) so larger values bubble toward the root
Negate every value on push and re-negate on pop — keeps the min-heap logic intact
Sift-up on extract-max instead of sift-down — only the operation, not the comparators, changes
questions.explain: The index math is identical; only the ordering comparisons flip — a max-heap keeps the largest at the root by reversing every `<`/`>` in the sift logic.

questions.q: You need repeated 'give me the current min, then add more items' on a changing dataset. Why a heap over a sorted array?
options: A heap keeps the full ordering of all n elements, while a sorted array only orders adjacent pairs
Insert is O(log n) on a heap vs O(n) to keep a sorted array sorted; you only pay for the min you actually extract
Binary search on a sorted array is O(log n), but it can't locate the insertion point in less than O(n) due to shifting — and a heap avoids the shift entirely with O(1) access
A heap's extract-min is O(1) since the min is at heap[0], whereas a sorted array's first-element removal is O(n)
questions.explain: A heap gives O(log n) insert and O(log n) extract-min without maintaining a total order; inserting into a sorted array to stay sorted is O(n) per insert.
